opening.headline: We explain what you should keep in your evaluation records and safety settings history so you can later prove that you evaluated your AI before launch.
body: When asked at a release approval meeting, “Do you have evidence that this chatbot has been sufficiently evaluated?”, if you only remember “I used it several times and it was good,” that is not evidence. It must remain not only the fact that an evaluation was made, but also which object was evaluated and with what data and criteria.

In this class, we will look at the types of evaluation and design principles described by Google and OpenAI documentation, and read code to see what and how the Gemini API's safety settings (safety_settings) prevent. Next, we summarize the items to be included in the evaluation record and the meaning of reproducibility, and use examples to confirm why the history of changes in safety settings is necessary to trace the cause.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of assessment records and safety settings
You can distinguish the items to be included in the evaluation record.

screens.title: The results of the pre-launch evaluation must be proven.
screens.lead: Read a scene from the launch approval meeting: It is good to look at the differences between the evidence that the team can provide and the evidence that executives require.

visual.alt: A scene where an executive asks a question at a conference table and an empty folder is placed in front of the team.
labels: Is there evidence that this chatbot has been sufficiently evaluated?
I used it several times and it was good
Evaluation + evaluation record + safety settings history = proof

paragraphs: an executive asks during a launch approval meeting. “Is there evidence that this chatbot has been sufficiently evaluated?” The team tried it several times and felt it was okay, but there was no documentation left about which questions were asked and which model version was reviewed and according to which criteria.

The situation becomes more difficult when a complaint with inadequate response comes in a month later. It is necessary to determine whether the conditions are the same at the time of evaluation and now, whether safety settings have changed, and whether the evaluation data differs from actual use, because there is no standard for comparison.

So proof consists of three things. The assessment itself, the assessment history that allows you to double-check that assessment, and the change history that shows what safety settings the service has been operating under. This class covers these three in turn.

screens.outro: First, let's recall our team's current record.

screens.title: Are you documenting the evaluation results?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit an answer, so think about your team first and then click.

items.prompt: Are you documenting the evaluation results?
items.answer: If you only share results via chat or verbally, they lose ground over time. In addition to the results, you need to know what questions were asked and what responses were given so that you can read them again later. The habit of leaving a document is more important than the format of the document.

items.prompt: Does it say which model version and settings it was evaluated on?
items.answer: Even services with the same name will have different results if the model version, system directives, or safety settings change. Without this information, we will not know if the results of the evaluation are grounds for current services.

items.prompt: If we run the same evaluation again, will we get the same conclusion?
items.answer: Generative AI can produce different outputs even with the same input. Therefore, information must be left so that the same evaluation can be performed again under the same conditions, and this property is called reproducibility. It's a central concept to this lesson, so we'll return to it later.

screens.outro: Now that we've checked the current status, let's take a look at what types of assessments are available.

screens.title: Four types of safety assessments
screens.lead: The following cards explain the types of safety assessments described by Google's Generative Responsible AI Toolkit and the evaluation principles in the OpenAI Guide. Selecting a card flips it over, and selecting the right arrow moves to the next card.

cards.back: An evaluation performed while training and fine-tuning the model. See how your model stacks up against launch baselines and whether the mitigations you've applied are effective. Check your model against a set of adversarial questions targeting a specific policy or against external academic benchmarks.

An evaluation for governance and review purposes, usually performed by a group outside the development team at the end of a major phase. Each form is standardized and the dataset is strictly managed. Only summarized insights are returned to the training, so the assessment itself is not compromised.

It is an adversarial test in which a team of experts from multiple fields, including safety, policy, and security, attacks an AI system. It is characterized by a less structured structure than the previous evaluations. Weaknesses discovered here are used to reduce risk and improve assessment methods.

An assessment performed by an independent, external subject matter expert to identify limitations. External groups can design their own assessments and push the limits of the model. It’s a means of identifying perspectives that your internal team may be missing.

The OpenAI guide explains that generative AI can produce different outputs from the same input, making traditional software testing alone insufficient. Evaluations are structured tests that check the system amidst this volatility. Numerical results should be read with human judgment.

screens.outro: Now that we know the types of evaluations, let's read the code for the safety settings that need to be set along with the evaluation.

screens.title: Safety Settings: What and How to Prevent
screens.lead: Below is an example of specifying safety settings in the Gemini API and what the error looks like when blocked. Check out the explanation on the right to see what each line determines and what symptoms occur if the values ​​are misaligned.

data.code:
from google import genai

client = genai.Client()

interaction = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-3.8-flash",
    input="Some potentially unsafe prompt.",
    safety_settings=[
        {
            "type": "hate_speech",
            "threshold": "block_low_and_above",
        }
    ],
)

print(interaction.output_text)

#If blocked, the request will fail with an HTTP 400 error and
#The code in the error tells you the reason for the block.
#Example: "code": "safety"

notes.note: This is a line that passes the safety settings list safety_settings along with the input. This list is passed from request to request, so the values ​​may vary across multiple calling code locations. If the values ​​are different during evaluation and operation, the evaluation results cannot serve as the basis for operation actions.

It is a pair of harm category (type) and blocking threshold (threshold). Setting hate_speech to block_low_and_above blocks content that has more than a low probability of being hate speech. Relaxing the threshold allows more responses to pass, making this value part of your safety policy.

This is the part that reads the output text. If blocked, no response is returned, so you must have code to treat it as an error before reaching this line. If you don't handle the error, it appears to the user as an unexplained failure.

If blocked, the request will fail with HTTP 400 and the blocked content will not be returned. The code in the error tells you the reason, jailbreak, prohibited_content, blocklist are cases where input is blocked. This error log provides evidence of how your setup behaves during production.

screens.outro: Now that you've read what safety settings mean, let's move on to the evaluation record form, tabulating the rules for thresholds and defaults.

screens.title: Commentary: Items to include in your evaluation record
screens.lead: The table below is an example of a chatbot launch evaluation record. Read along with the instructor's explanation to see what you write in each item and what questions you will not be able to answer if you leave it blank.

visual.alt: Illustration of the evaluation record form items stacked from top to bottom, with a reproducibility arrow leading to the right.
labels: Can be run again under the same conditions = Reproducibility

data.caption: Example of customer service chatbot launch evaluation record
columns: Questions that cannot be answered if left blank
rows: Model name and version, system directives, tool definitions, and safety settings
Is the service currently in operation the same as the evaluated target?
The source and number of question bundles and whether they reflect the actual distribution of inquiries.
Is the evaluation representative of actual use?
Accuracy and safety criteria, whether automatic scoring or human judgment, and whether automatic scoring was calibrated by human judgment.
Based on what criteria were the results obtained?
Passing criteria, scoring values for each item, and failure cases
Was it at a level where it could be released?
To what extent is it not guaranteed?
Who made the decision to release and on what basis?
data.notes: Reproducibility is the degree to which information remains so that the evaluation can be repeated with the same subject, same data, and same settings. The OpenAI guide identifies evaluations that rely on intuition and evaluations made with data different from actual traffic as anti-patterns to avoid, and recommends that automatic scoring indicators be calibrated with human evaluations. The table above translates this principle into record items.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the record items, let's take an example of what happens when there is no history.

screens.title: Explanation: Why do we keep a history of safety settings changes?
screens.lead: The instructor tracks complaints step by step one month after launch. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Case: Inadequate Response Complaint
steps.body: A month after launch, complaints were received that the customer service chatbot provided inappropriate responses. The evaluation upon release was a pass. If so, we need to determine what has changed since launch. Divide the candidate causes into three and check them one by one.

steps.title: Cause Candidate 1: Model Version
steps.body: Check if the model version has changed. If the evaluation record lists a version for the item being evaluated, you can compare it to the current operating version. Without records, you won't even know if the assessment corresponds to your current service.

steps.title: Candidate cause 2: Relax safety settings
steps.body: See if anyone has relaxed the threshold for categories like hate_speech. In models after Gemini 2.5, the default value of the adjustable filter is Off and you are instructed to adjust it only when necessary, so if the value has changed, there must be a history of who changed it, when and why. Core harms, such as child safety, are always blocked and cannot be adjusted.

steps.title: Candidate cause 3: Differences between evaluation data and actual use
steps.body: Check whether the set of questions you wrote during the evaluation differs from the pattern that customers are actually asking now. If customer inquiry types change after launch, the initial evaluation may not be representative of the current situation. This is the reason for the anti-pattern guidance to match evaluation data to actual traffic.

steps.title: Detect quality changes during operation
steps.body: Google's online monitor continuously evaluates the quality of running agents, detecting quality drift as user behavior or external data changes. This decline can occur even if your model is the same, and you can set up quality alerts to be notified when your model falls below the standard.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: Having a change history and evaluation record can help you narrow down which of the three candidates was the cause and whose decision it was. If there is no evaluation, it will be as if it never happened. Unrecorded evaluations do not serve as evidence.

screens.outro: I will summarize what I found in the case in one paragraph.

screens.title: An evaluation that is not recorded is as if it does not exist.
screens.lead: Let's tie the contents of this class into one principle. Read the paragraph below and move on to the final summary.

paragraphs: Evaluation is not something you do once and ends, but it also includes leaving the results so that they can be re-read and returned to later. The evaluation record should consist of the evaluation object, evaluation data, indicators and judgment methods, results, limitations, and approvals, and should be specific enough to be repeated under the same conditions.

Safety settings are part of your policy, even if you leave them to their defaults. If you adjust the threshold, record the adjusted value and reason, and keep a history of each change. It is important to be able to compare whether the settings during evaluation and the settings during operation are the same so that the evaluation results become the basis for operation.

Finally, evaluation isn't just necessary before launch. As models and usage patterns change, quality also changes, so evaluations must continue and records must be kept during operation. Don't judge that a single number is enough, but leave the conditions and human judgment that created the number together.

In summary, the evidence is stacked in three layers. At the bottom is a history that allows you to rerun the assessment, above that is a change history that shows what settings the service has been running under, and at the top is monitoring to keep a check on quality during operation. Evaluation records provide the basis for release approval, change history provides the basis for tracing the cause behind an incident, and monitoring ensures that the evaluation remains valid over time. If even one of the three layers is empty, the saying “it was okay at the time” loses ground. Manage the three layers together by deciding on a person in charge and an update time, and update the records whenever the model or settings change.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: A good standard for evaluation records is whether the same evaluation can be repeated even after the person in charge changes.

checks.intro: Check out the types of assessments and safety settings concepts. Just match each term with an appropriate explanation. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Match the concepts of assessment and safety settings with explanations.
left: Core harms such as child safety
right: A value that determines at what level to block each category of harm.
Groups outside the development team perform key steps for governance purposes
Find weaknesses with less structured adversarial attacks
checks.correctFeedback: A clear distinction was made between the nature of the assessment and the safety setting.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some connections are off. Find out who is doing the evaluation and for what purpose, and divide the settings into adjusted and non-adjusted values.
checks.explain: The evaluations have different purposes and performers, and safety settings are divided into adjustable values and core harms that are always blocked.

checks.intro: Think of examples of commentary and choose what records are needed.
checks.q: A month after launch, complaints of inadequate response were received. What does it take to tell if someone has relaxed the hate_speech threshold?
options: All you need is a list of question sets used in the evaluation.
Change history of safety set values
List of people who attended the launch approval meeting
One indicator of declining quality in online monitors
checks.correctFeedback: You correctly point out that a change history is needed to mask configuration changes.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This data cannot determine whether the threshold has changed.
checks.explain: Because safety settings are part of a policy, you need a history of changes to narrow down who relaxed them and when. Without history, it is difficult to trace cause and responsibility.

wrong.0: Question sets are used to view problems in assessment data and are different clues than changing settings.
wrong.2: The attendee list does not tell you whether settings have changed.
wrong.3: Quality degradation indicators only detect changes and do not tell you who changed the settings.

glossary.def: This is a document that describes the evaluation object, data, indicators, results, limitations, and approval. Be specific enough to return to the same evaluation later.
This is a value that determines the safe behavior of the service, such as a blocking threshold for each hazard category. The adjusted values ​​are part of your safety policy.
This is an activity to check the safety of AI, such as development evaluation, assurance evaluation, red team, and external evaluation. The carrying out and purpose are different.
This is the property of being able to compare the results by repeating the evaluation with the same target, data, and settings.
This is a phenomenon in which the performance of an agent during operation deteriorates over time as user behavior or data changes.

misconceptions.myth: Once you get a good result, the evaluation is over.
misconceptions.fact: Models and usage patterns change over time. Evaluation should continue during operation, and the results and conditions should be recorded.

misconceptions.myth: Just one number is enough to record your rating.
misconceptions.fact: The numbers in the evaluation results should be read in conjunction with what data and standards they were created from and how they were compared with human judgment. The OpenAI guide also advises combining metrics with human judgment.

misconceptions.myth: Leave the safety settings to their defaults and there is nothing to record.
misconceptions.fact: In models where tunable filters default to Off, relying on that default is also a policy decision. You should record whether you changed the value, why you changed it, and if you use the default value.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: An evaluation that is not recorded is as good as none.
The evaluation record must be specific enough to consist of targets, data, indicators, results, limitations, and acknowledgments and be reproducible.
Because safety settings are part of a policy, they leave a history of changes.
Evaluation continues during operation to detect any decline in quality.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Can we repeat the same evaluation just based on our evaluation records? Think about what, if anything, is missing.
